lesson.intro: Most CCNA exhibits are troubleshooting questions in disguise: something is broken, and the clue sits in one line of output. This lesson gives you a method, then the commands that matter layer by layer, the fields to read first and the faults each reveals.
objectives: Choose a troubleshooting method that fits the symptoms
Interpret ping and traceroute output to locate where a path fails
Find Layer 1 and Layer 2 faults in interface, VLAN, trunk, CDP, STP and EtherChannel output
Diagnose routing, OSPF, HSRP, NAT, DHCP, NTP, ACL and port security problems from exhibits

sections.title: A method beats guessing
sections.key: Define the problem precisely, pick a method that fits the evidence, change one thing at a time, and verify that the original symptom is gone.
sections.body:
A user says "the network is down." Before you type a command, make it precise: which host, which destination, what works, since when. "PC1 in VLAN 10 cannot reach 10.2.2.50 but can reach its gateway" already rules out half the network.

[[visual]]

Whatever the method, run the same loop, and change one thing at a time or you will never know which change fixed it:

[[visual 2]]

Exam simlets may give you only user EXEC (R1>), so no `show running-config`. Learn the commands that reveal configuration anyway, and filter the configuration when you can see it:

[[visual 3]]

[[code]]

rows: Layer 1: cables and interface status, then climb
Symptoms are broad or physical. Thorough but slow
Every port on a newly installed switch is dead
Lower layers clearly work and one service fails
Only DNS lookups fail; everything else works
You do not know the layer. Fastest for most exam scenarios
A ping to the IP works, so Layers 1 to 3 are fine: go up. It fails: go down
Host, access switch, trunk, gateway, each router; traceroute does part of it
Something similar works. Most CCNA faults are mismatches
The other end of a trunk, the HSRP peer, a branch from the same template

Gather information with show commands and tests
Form a hypothesis about the cause
Make one change to test it

steps.no: Undo the change and form a new hypothesis

Which networks OSPF is routing for

Each matching parent line with all its indented children

sections.code:
R1# show running-config | section router ospf
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

R1# show running-config | include helper|access-group
 ip helper-address 10.9.9.9
 ip access-group 10 out
sections.tip: Output filters are case-sensitive. In the running configuration, | include Helper finds nothing while | include helper finds ip helper-address.
sections.pitfall: Changing several settings at once. If the symptom disappears you do not know which change fixed it, and an unneeded change can cause the next outage. Make one change, then retest.

check.question: A ping from PC1 to the server's IP address works, but browsing to the server by name fails. Using divide and conquer, where do you look next?
choices: Down the stack: cabling and interface counters on the access switch
Up the stack: the DNS settings and the application
The trunk between the access switch and the distribution switch
The default gateway's routing table
check.explanation: A working ping to the IP address proves Layers 1 to 3 along the path, so divide and conquer moves up: name resolution and the application. Rechecking cables or routes would retest what the ping already proved.

sections.title: Ping and traceroute: reading the symbols
sections.key: In ping, `!` is a reply, `.` a timeout and `U` an unreachable from a router. In traceroute the fault lies just after the last hop that answers.
sections.body:
An IOS ping sends five echo requests with a 2-second timeout and prints one character for each:

[[visual]]

A `U` is good news: the router that sent it is reachable, and it is the one with the missing route or ACL.

A router's ping uses its outgoing interface as the source. It never tests the route back to the users' subnet, ACLs that match the users' addresses, or the user's own gateway setting. Use an **extended ping**: `ping 10.2.2.50 source g0/1`, or `ping` alone and answer the prompts.

**traceroute** sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on; each router that drops one for TTL reports its address:

[[visual 2]]

`*` means no answer: the next router never got the probe, or its reply cannot find a way back. `!H`, `!N` and `!A` (host unreachable, network unreachable, administratively prohibited) say why a router refused.

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

rows: Nothing came back before the timeout: dropped somewhere, in either direction
A router returned ICMP destination unreachable: no route, or an ACL rejected it
Rare: could not fragment, source quench (too busy), unknown packet type, lifetime exceeded
Normal on a first attempt: the first echo timed out while a device resolved a MAC with ARP
A router is rejecting the packets and rate-limits its unreachables, so every other probe times out
Often two load-shared paths, one of them broken

visual.title: What the exhibit means
visual.caption: R2 answers hop 1, then rejects the hop 2 probes itself. Its routing table is the next thing to check.

sections.code:
R1# ping 10.3.3.10
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.3.3.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
U.U.U
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)

R1# traceroute 10.3.3.10
Tracing the route to 10.3.3.10
  1 10.1.12.2 4 msec 4 msec 4 msec
  2 10.1.12.2 !H  *  !H
sections.deeper:
Silence is different from a refusal. If hop 2 answers and then only `* * *` follows, the hop 2 router did forward the probes; had it lacked a route, it would have sent `!H` or `!N`. Check the next link, the next router, and that router's return route.

Windows uses `tracert`, which sends ICMP echoes, while IOS `traceroute` sends UDP probes, so an ACL can block one and not the other. Pinging a host on the same LAN from its router proves the LAN works but not the host's default gateway setting, because the reply never leaves the subnet.
sections.tip: A row of periods tells you that something dropped the packets, not where. Follow up with traceroute, or ping each hop in turn, to find where the path stops.
sections.pitfall: Testing from the router with a standard ping and declaring the path good. The return route to the users' subnet and ACLs matching their addresses are never tested. Use an extended ping sourced from the LAN interface.

check.question: What does the ping result .!!!! usually mean on a first attempt?
choices: One of the five links along the path is down
An ACL denies the first packet of every flow
The path works; the first echo timed out while ARP resolved a MAC address
The destination rate-limits replies after the first one
check.explanation: Four replies prove the path works in both directions. The first echo was lost while a device on the path waited for an ARP reply, which is why the same ping repeated shows !!!!!.

sections.title: Layer 1: interface state and error counters
sections.key: Down/down is physical, up/down is Layer 2, err-disabled needs its cause fixed and a bounce, and a duplex mismatch stays connected while late collisions climb.
sections.body:
Start bottom-up with one line per interface: `show ip interface brief` on a router (line status is Layer 1, protocol is Layer 2), or `show interfaces status` on a switch, which adds VLAN, duplex and speed.

[[visual]]

A **speed mismatch** takes the link down. A **duplex mismatch** does not: the port shows connected and performs badly.

The `a-` prefix means autonegotiated, so `a-half` on a gigabit port is a warning: the neighbor has speed and duplex hard-coded, so this side senses the speed and falls back to half duplex. Fix it by letting both ends autonegotiate, or configuring both identically.

[[code]]

Then read the counters in `show interfaces`:

[[visual 2]]

Counters add up since boot or `clear counters`, so one number says little: clear them, wait, and look again.

rows: No cable, a bad cable, far end shut down or off, or a speed mismatch
Check the cable and the far end; match the speeds
Not seen on switch Ethernet ports
A Layer 2 problem, such as mismatched encapsulation on a serial link
Match the encapsulation on both ends
Port security, BPDU guard or an EtherChannel misconfiguration
Fix the cause, then `shutdown` and `no shutdown`
Frames under 64 bytes, often from collisions
A total that includes runts, giants, CRC errors and more
Frames whose FCS check failed. Rising with zero collisions: a bad cable or interference
A collision after the first 64 bytes: almost always a duplex mismatch, counted on the half-duplex side

SW1# show interfaces status
Port   Name           Status       Vlan  Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1  Uplink to SW2  connected    trunk a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/2                 notconnect   1       auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/3  Printer        err-disabled 10      auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/4                 disabled     1       auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

SW1# show interfaces g0/1 | include duplex|errors|collision
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     0 output errors, 1874 collisions, 2 interface resets
     0 babbles, 431 late collision, 0 deferred
sections.tip: show interfaces status says err-disabled; show interfaces shows the same port as down, line protocol is down (err-disabled). The log or show port-security interface tells you which feature did it.
sections.pitfall: Trusting connected. Up/up only proves the link is physically alive; a duplex mismatch, CRC errors or the wrong access VLAN all hide behind a connected port.

check.question: In the exhibit, SW1 Gi0/1 shows connected, a-half and a-100, and its late collision counter keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A speed mismatch with SW2
Electrical interference on the cable
SW2 Gi0/1 is administratively down
A duplex mismatch: SW2 has speed and duplex set manually, so autonegotiation fails
check.explanation: Half duplex learned by autonegotiation on a gigabit port, plus late collisions, is the duplex mismatch signature. A speed mismatch would bring the link down (notconnect), and interference shows up as CRC errors without collisions.

sections.title: Access ports: VLANs, switchport and the MAC table
sections.key: A connected host that cannot reach its own subnet is usually in the wrong VLAN, or in a VLAN that does not exist on the switch.
sections.body:
Three commands find it:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In the exhibit Gi0/5 is in VLAN 99 (PARKING) instead of VLAN 10 (SALES), and PC5's MAC was learned in VLAN 99. The port is connected and the host is fine; it is isolated in the wrong broadcast domain. The fix is `switchport access vlan 10` on Gi0/5.

[[visual 2]]

rows: Each VLAN, its status and its access ports
Which VLAN the host's port is in
**Trunks are never listed.** A VLAN that is act/lshut or suspended forwards nothing
Operational Mode (actual) against Administrative Mode (configured); Access Mode VLAN and Voice VLAN
`Access Mode VLAN: 30 (Inactive)`: VLAN 30 does not exist, so the port forwards nothing and drops out of `show vlan brief`
The VLAN and port each MAC was learned on
A MAC learned on a trunk port: the host sits behind another switch

visual.caption: Gi0/1 is missing from show vlan brief because it is a trunk, which is normal.

SW1# show vlan brief
VLAN Name           Status    Ports

1    default        active    Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4
10   SALES          active    Gi0/6, Gi0/7, Gi0/8
20   ENG            active    Gi0/9, Gi0/10
99   PARKING        active    Gi0/5

SW1# show mac address-table interface g0/5
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----

sections.deeper: Two more access-port traps. When you type `switchport access vlan 30` for a VLAN that does not exist, IOS creates it for you; but if someone later deletes VLAN 30, its ports go inactive and vanish from show vlan brief. And a port with an IP phone carries two VLANs, the access VLAN for the PC and the voice VLAN for the phone, so check both values in show interfaces switchport.
sections.tip: Read Operational Mode, not Administrative Mode, in show interfaces switchport. The administrative value is what you asked for; the operational value is what you got.
sections.pitfall: Looking for the uplink in show vlan brief and concluding it is broken because it is missing. Trunks are listed by show interfaces trunk, not show vlan brief.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: PC in the wrong VLAN
activity.prompt: A connected port leaves its user isolated. Start with show vlan brief and show interfaces status, find the port in the wrong VLAN, and fix it without creating new VLANs.

check.question: A PC port appears in no VLAN in show vlan brief and is not a trunk. show interfaces g0/8 switchport shows Access Mode VLAN: 30 (Inactive). What is wrong?
choices: VLAN 30 does not exist on this switch, so the port cannot forward
The port is operating as a trunk
VLAN 30 is configured as the native VLAN
Port security has err-disabled the port
check.explanation: Inactive means the access VLAN is not defined (or was deleted). Ports in a missing VLAN drop out of show vlan brief and forward nothing until you create the VLAN or assign an existing one.

sections.title: Between switches: trunks, CDP and LLDP
sections.key: show interfaces trunk lists only trunking ports and three narrowing VLAN lists; the list a VLAN drops out of says whether configuration, a missing VLAN or STP removed it.
sections.body:
When hosts in one VLAN cannot talk across two switches, check the link between them. Compare both ends: each must allow the VLAN and know it.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In the exhibit VLAN 10 was removed from the allowed list, and CDP reports a **native VLAN** mismatch (1 against 99), which merges two VLANs for untagged frames.

[[visual 2]]

**CDP** and **LLDP** show who is really on the other end, so check the cabling matches the diagram. `show cdp neighbors detail` also gives the neighbor's IP address, platform, IOS version and native VLAN. LLDP needs `lldp run`; CDP is on by default.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: The three lists in show interfaces trunk

steps.label: 1. Vlans allowed on trunk
steps.detail: 1-4094 minus removals by `switchport trunk allowed vlan`. Missing here: configuration removed it

steps.label: 2. Allowed and active in management domain
steps.detail: Minus VLANs not defined or shut down on this switch. Missing here: create or enable it

steps.label: 3. In spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
steps.detail: Minus VLANs STP blocks on this port, or VTP pruned. Missing only here: usually STP doing its job

visual.title: When the link is not trunking right
rows: Port missing from `show interfaces trunk`, Operational Mode: static access
Not trunking: dynamic auto on both ends waits forever. Set `switchport mode trunk` on at least one end
Link up, native VLAN works, every other VLAN silently dropped
One side `trunk` with `switchport nonegotiate`, the other side not trunking
Native VLANs differ; set the same native VLAN on both ends

visual.title: Reading CDP on SW1
visual.caption: SW1's entry for SW3 shows `Interface: GigabitEthernet0/1`, your own port, and `Port ID (outgoing port): GigabitEthernet0/3`, SW3's port. LLDP calls them Local Intf and Port id.

sections.code:

sections.tip: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10 adds one VLAN. switchport trunk allowed vlan 10 replaces the whole list and can cut every other VLAN off the trunk.
sections.pitfall: Reading Interface in show cdp neighbors detail as the neighbor's port. Interface is yours; Port ID (outgoing port) belongs to the neighbor.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: VLAN 10 cannot cross the trunk
activity.prompt: The trunk is up, VLAN 20 works and VLAN 10 does not, and CDP keeps complaining. Use show interfaces trunk and show cdp neighbors detail to find both faults, then fix them without removing VLANs 20 or 99.

check.question: VLAN 30 appears in the first and second VLAN lists of show interfaces trunk for Gi0/24, but not in the third. What is the most likely reason?
choices: VLAN 30 was removed from the allowed list
Spanning tree is blocking VLAN 30 on Gi0/24
VLAN 30 does not exist on this switch
Gi0/24 is not trunking
check.explanation: Being in list 2 proves the VLAN is allowed, exists and is active. The third list removes VLANs in an STP blocking state (or VTP pruned), so STP is the likely reason, and that may be exactly what the design intends.

sections.title: Spanning tree and EtherChannel
sections.key: Chase root ports to find the root, recognize each guard's fingerprint, and read EtherChannel flags: P bundled, I stand-alone, s suspended.
sections.body:
STP rarely fails outright; usually the wrong switch is root, or a port you expected to forward is blocking.

In `show spanning-tree vlan 10` the **Root ID** block describes the root bridge, plus your cost and root port toward it. The **Bridge ID** block describes the switch you are on. On the root itself it says This bridge is the root.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

In the exhibit Po1 is up (SU) on Gi0/23 alone; Gi0/24 is suspended until its settings match.

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Find the root bridge

steps.label: Run `show spanning-tree vlan 10`
Does it say This bridge is the root?
steps.yes: Found it: the root has no root port

steps.label: Use CDP to find the switch on the other end of that port
Run the command on that neighbor

visual.loop: Repeat: each root port points one hop closer

visual.title: Guard fingerprints
rows: A PortFast port receives a BPDU
Remove the cause, then `shutdown` and `no shutdown`
By itself, once those BPDUs stop
A nondesignated port stops receiving BPDUs

rows: Stand-alone: did not negotiate with the other end
Suspended: its settings differ from the other members
visual.caption: Members must match speed, duplex, and the access VLAN or trunk settings (mode, allowed list, native VLAN).

Interface    Role Sts Cost   Prio.Nbr Type
Gi0/1        Root FWD 4      128.1    P2p

sections.deeper:
Port roles in the bottom half: Root (toward the root), Desg (designated, forwarding onto a segment), Altn and Back (alternate and backup, blocking). States: FWD, BLK and LRN. P2p Edge marks a PortFast port.

Why mode on facing LACP or PAgP is worse than no channel: the on side forwards as one logical link while the other side treats the ports as separate links, which risks a loop. The switch detects it and err-disables the ports instead.
sections.tip: In the Root ID block, Cost and Port appear only on non-root switches. If you see This bridge is the root instead, you are logged in to the root.
sections.pitfall: Reading the Bridge ID priority as the root's priority. The top block (Root ID) describes the root bridge; the second block (Bridge ID) describes the switch you are logged in to.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: EtherChannel will not bundle
activity.prompt: Both links to SW2 are err-disabled and Po1 is down. Use show etherchannel summary and show interfaces status err-disabled to find the two faults, fix them, and bring both links into Po1 as (P).

check.question: In the exhibit, Po1 shows (SU), Gi0/23 shows (P) and Gi0/24 shows (s). What does that mean?
choices: Both ports are bundled and Gi0/24 is an LACP hot-standby link
The EtherChannel is down and both ports run as separate links
Gi0/24 is suspended because its settings do not match; Po1 runs on Gi0/23 only
Gi0/24 has been converted to a Layer 3 port
check.explanation: P means bundled and s means suspended, which IOS does when a member port's configuration differs from the channel (for example a different allowed VLAN list). SU says Po1 is a working Layer 2 channel. Hot-standby would show H.

sections.title: Layer 3: the routing table and default gateways
sections.key: Every routed packet needs a correct host address, mask and gateway, a route at every hop, and a route back. Routers choose the longest prefix match before comparing AD.
sections.body:
On the host (`ipconfig`, or `ip addr` on Linux), a gateway outside the host's own subnet, a wrong mask or a 169.254.x.x address (no DHCP answer) explains most single-host failures.

On each router, read `show ip route`: the code (C connected, L local, S static, O OSPF, `*` candidate default), the prefix, [administrative distance/metric], the next hop and the interface.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A packet to 10.2.2.100 falls outside the /26 (.0 to .63), so only the /24 matches and it goes via 10.1.12.2. Gateway of last resort is not set means no default route: unknown destinations are dropped and the sender gets U.

[[visual 3]]

steps.label: List every route that matches
The longest prefix wins
AD only breaks ties for the same prefix

visual.title: Classic Layer 3 faults
rows: Host reaches its own subnet only
Default gateway outside its subnet, or a wrong mask
Static route missing from the table
Its next hop is unreachable: that interface is down, so its connected route vanished
Floating static always in the table, `!.!.!` pings
Same AD as the primary, so the router load-shares across both paths and one fails
One VLAN cannot reach its router-on-a-stick gateway
Wrong `encapsulation dot1Q` tag on that subinterface (it still shows up/up), or the switch port is not trunking that VLAN
Pings time out (`.....`) instead of U
A missing return route on some router

sections.pitfall: Picking the route with the lowest AD before checking prefix length. Longest prefix match comes first; AD only compares routes to exactly the same prefix.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: static routes on a transit router
activity.prompt: Three static routing faults on R2 break traffic in three different ways. Read show ip route static closely, including every next hop and distance, fix all three, and prove it with pings.

check.question: Using the exhibit, which route does R1 use for a packet to 10.2.2.100?
choices: None, so the packet is dropped
Both routes, load balanced
check.explanation: 10.2.2.0/26 covers 10.2.2.0 to 10.2.2.63, so 10.2.2.100 does not match it. The only matching route is the OSPF /24 via 10.1.12.2.

sections.title: OSPF neighbors and HSRP
sections.key: A missing OSPF neighbor means the adjacency failed; a FULL neighbor with a missing route means the subnet is not advertised. Two HSRP Actives cannot hear each other.
sections.body:
OSPF problems fall into two buckets, and the show commands tell you which one you have:

[[visual]]

For a missing neighbor, compare both routers' `show ip ospf interface`. Hellos are rejected unless all of this holds:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

In the exhibit R1 is a DROTHER: FULL with the BDR, 2WAY with the other DROTHER (fine), and stuck in EXSTART with the DR, 4.4.4.4, so compare the two MTUs.

**HSRP** gives hosts one virtual gateway shared by two routers. `show standby brief` lists group, priority, P (preempt configured), state, active and standby routers and virtual IP.

[[visual 3]]

steps.label: Is the router missing from `show ip ospf neighbor`?
steps.yes: The hellos are rejected: check the list below

steps.label: Stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE?
2WAY/DROTHER?
steps.yes: Normal between two DROTHERs on a LAN: they go FULL only with the DR and BDR

steps.label: FULL, but a subnet is missing from `show ip route`?
steps.yes: Not advertised: check `show ip protocols` or `show ip ospf interface brief`

rows: Interfaces up/up, in the same subnet
Area 0 on one side and area 1 on the other never meet
Hello 10 against hello 5 hides the neighbor completely
Passive sends no hellos, but still advertises the subnet

visual.title: Reading show standby brief
rows: One Active, one Standby, same group and virtual IP on both
They cannot hear each other's hellos: a Layer 2 problem between them, or mismatched group numbers
Higher-priority router is back but stays Standby
Preemption is missing on it (no P): add `standby 10 preempt`

sections.tip: Neighbor ID is the neighbor's router ID; Address is its interface IP on the shared link. Exhibit questions often swap the two in the answer choices.
sections.pitfall: Treating 2WAY/DROTHER as a broken adjacency. On a LAN with a DR and BDR, DROTHERs stay in 2WAY with each other by design.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: OSPF is not advertising the LAN
activity.prompt: R1 is FULL with R2, yet R2 never learns R1's LAN. Use show ip protocols and show ip ospf interface brief to see what OSPF covers, then add what is missing without breaking the adjacency.

check.question: In the exhibit, why is neighbor 4.4.4.4 most likely stuck in EXSTART?
choices: Its interface MTU does not match R1's
Its hello timer does not match R1's
It is in a different OSPF area
Its router ID duplicates R1's
check.explanation: Hello timer and area mismatches stop the neighbor from appearing at all, because the hellos are rejected. A neighbor that reached EXSTART passed the hello checks and is stuck exchanging database descriptions, which is the classic MTU mismatch symptom.

sections.title: IP services: NAT, DHCP and NTP
sections.key: An empty NAT table points to swapped inside and outside, the ACL or a missing overload; 169.254 clients need a helper address; NTP reach 0 means no replies.
sections.body:
**NAT.** `show ip nat translations` lists four addresses per entry:

[[visual 4]]

With PAT, many inside locals share one inside global, told apart by port:

[[code]]

[[visual]]

**DHCP.** A client with a 169.254.x.x address never got an answer.

[[visual 2]]

**NTP.** `show ntp status` says Clock is synchronized (with stratum and reference) or Clock is unsynchronized. Read `show ntp associations` like this:

[[visual 3]]

In the exhibit R1 is unsynchronized with reach 0: it has never heard from 10.9.9.123, so check routing, ACLs and the server address. Synchronizing takes a few minutes, so wait before calling it broken.

activity.title: Troubleshoot: NAT is translating nothing
activity.prompt: PAT is configured, the default route is there, and the translation table stays empty. Use show ip nat statistics to see which interface IOS treats as inside, fix it, and watch translations appear.

check.question: In the exhibit, what is the inside local address of the host whose DNS query was translated?
check.explanation: The UDP entry to 8.8.8.8 port 53 is the DNS query. Its inside local column shows the host's private address, 192.168.1.12; 203.0.113.2 is the shared inside global address, and 8.8.8.8 is the outside server.

sections.title: Filters: ACLs and port security
sections.key: For ACLs, find where and in which direction, read top down to the first match, and confirm with counters. For port security, read Port Status, violation mode and count.
sections.body:
When pings and routes look right but specific traffic still fails, suspect a filter.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In the exhibit ACL 101 filters traffic arriving on R2 G0/0. Hosts in 10.1.1.0/24 reach the web server on port 80 (line 10), everything else they send is denied (line 20), OSPF passes (line 30), and other subnets hit the implicit deny.

[[visual 2]]

For **port security**, `show port-security interface` gives Port Status, Violation Mode, Maximum MAC Addresses, the Last Source Address:Vlan that broke the rule, and the Security Violation Count.

[[visual 3]]

Send test traffic and watch which counter climbs

sections.tip: While troubleshooting, add an explicit deny ip any any at the end of an ACL. It behaves like the implicit deny but has a match counter, so you can see what is being dropped.
sections.pitfall: Looking only at Port Status. In restrict and protect modes it stays Secure-up while frames are dropped, so check the violation count (restrict) or which MAC addresses were learned (protect).

activity.title: Troubleshoot: an ACL is blocking everything
activity.prompt: An ACL meant to block one subnet blocks every host. Read show access-lists, think about the invisible last line, and fix it so only 192.168.20.0/24 is denied.

check.question: In the exhibit, users in 10.1.1.0/24 can open http://10.2.2.50, but https://10.2.2.50 fails. Why?
choices: Line 20 denies it, because line 10 permits only TCP port 80 (www)
The implicit deny drops it, because it matches no line
Line 30 drops it because it is not OSPF
ACL 101 is applied outbound, so the HTTPS replies are dropped
check.explanation: HTTPS is TCP port 443, which does not match line 10 (eq www is port 80). The packet comes from 10.1.1.0/24, so line 20 matches and denies it before the implicit deny is reached. show ip interface shows the ACL is inbound.

keyTerms.definition: Start at Layer 1 (cables, interface status) and work up the layers until you find the fault.
Start at the application and work down; best when lower layers clearly work.
Start in the middle, usually with a ping, and move up or down depending on the result.
Check each device a packet crosses from source to destination, hop by hop.
Find the fault by comparing a broken device or link with a working one.
A router ping with options such as a chosen source interface, used to test the return route to a LAN.
An ICMP destination unreachable from a router with no route or a denying ACL; U.U.U shows rate limiting.
The ICMP message a router sends when it drops a packet whose TTL reached 0; traceroute uses it to list hops.
A port shut down by a feature such as port security, BPDU guard or EtherChannel misconfiguration; needs shutdown and no shutdown after the fix.
A collision after the first 64 bytes of a frame; today it almost always means a duplex mismatch.
A received frame that failed the FCS check; rising CRC counts without collisions point to cabling or interference.
The two ends of a trunk use different native VLANs; CDP logs %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH.
The state root guard puts a port in while superior BPDUs arrive; it clears by itself.
In show etherchannel summary: bundled, stand-alone (no negotiation partner) and suspended (settings mismatch).
An OSPF neighbor state; a neighbor stuck there or in EXCHANGE usually has an MTU mismatch.
An inside host's address before NAT (usually private) and after NAT (as the internet sees it).
ip helper-address on the client-facing interface relays DHCP broadcasts to a server in another subnet.
The port security status of a port err-disabled by a violation in shutdown mode.

summary: Define the problem, pick a method, change one thing at a time and verify the original symptom.
Ping: ! reply, . timeout, U a router refused; .!!!! is ARP. Extended ping tests the return route.
Down/down is physical, up/down is Layer 2, err-disabled needs a bounce; a-half with late collisions is duplex.
show vlan brief lists access ports only; the three trunk lists say who removed a VLAN; CDP Interface is yours.
Longest prefix first, then AD; EXSTART means MTU; two HSRP Actives cannot hear each other.
Check NAT inside and outside, helper placement, NTP reach, ACL order and counters, and port security mode.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: A colleague says "the branch cannot reach the file server." Explain how you would isolate the fault: which method you would start with, which commands you would run in what order, and what in each output would make you stop and fix something.

questions.question: Which troubleshooting method begins with cabling and interface status and works up through the layers?
choices: Top-down
Bottom-up
Divide and conquer
Compare configurations
questions.explanation: Bottom-up starts at Layer 1 and climbs. Top-down starts at the application; divide and conquer starts in the middle, usually with a ping.

questions.question: Match each troubleshooting method to the situation where it fits best.

pairs.right: A newly cabled switch where nothing works
Every application works except one web app
You ping first to decide whether to look up or down the stack
You check each hop between the host and the server in turn
Branch 2 works; branch 3, built from the same template, does not

questions.explanation: Pick the method from the evidence: broad physical symptoms suggest bottom-up, a single failing service top-down, an unknown layer divide and conquer, a multi-hop path follow the path, and a working twin compare configurations.

questions.question: Put the steps of a structured troubleshooting process in order.
items: Define the problem precisely: who, what, since when
Gather information with show commands and tests
Form a hypothesis about the cause
Make one change to test the hypothesis
Verify that the original symptom is gone
Document the cause and the fix
questions.explanation: Gather, hypothesize, change one thing, verify, document. Verifying against the original symptom (not just "the command took") is what proves the fix.

questions.question: Type the command that displays only the router ospf part of the running configuration, with all its subcommands.
questions.explanation: | section prints each matching parent line with its indented children. | include would show only the lines containing the word, without the network and router-id lines under them.

questions.question: In a simlet you only have user EXEC access (R1>) and must find which ACL is applied inbound on G0/0. Which command shows it?
choices: show running-config interface g0/0
show access-lists
show interfaces g0/0
show ip interface g0/0
questions.explanation: show ip interface lists Inbound access list and Outgoing access list per interface and runs in user EXEC. show running-config needs privileged EXEC, and show access-lists shows the ACL contents but not where it is applied.

questions.question: Match each IOS ping output character to its meaning.

pairs.right: The packet could not be fragmented
Source quench: the destination is too busy

questions.explanation: ! and . are the everyday ones. U is the useful failure: a router actively said it cannot deliver the packet, which tells you a route or ACL problem exists on that router.

questions.question: R1 pings host B for the first time. What is the most likely reason the first echo failed?
questions.code:
R1# ping 172.16.2.101
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 172.16.2.101, timeout is 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate is 80 percent (4/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/4 ms
choices: A device on the path was resolving a MAC address with ARP
Host B was rate-limiting replies
The route to 172.16.2.0 was flapping
An ACL denied the first packet
questions.explanation: The path clearly works (four replies). The first echo was lost while a router or host waited for an ARP reply, which is why a repeat of the same ping shows !!!!!.

questions.question: R3 (10.1.23.3) connects to R4, which owns 10.4.4.0/24. Based on the exhibit, where should you look first?
questions.code:
R1# traceroute 10.4.4.10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Tracing the route to 10.4.4.10
VRF info: (vrf in name/id, vrf out name/id)
  1 10.1.12.2 4 msec 4 msec 4 msec
  2 10.1.23.3 8 msec 8 msec 8 msec
  3  *  *  *
  4  *  *  *
  5  *  *  *
choices: R3's routing table, because R3 has no route to 10.4.4.0/24
Between R1 and R2, because the first hop answered fastest
Past R3: the R3 to R4 link, R4 itself, or R4's route back to R1
Nowhere; timeouts are normal at the end of every traceroute
questions.explanation: R3 forwarded the TTL 3 probes; if it had no route it would have answered with !H or !N. Silence after R3 means R4 never received them, or R4's TTL exceeded replies cannot get back to R1, so check the link, R4 and R4's return route.

questions.question: What does this ping output indicate?
questions.code:
R1# ping 10.5.5.5
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.5.5.5, timeout is 2 seconds:
U.U.U
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
choices: A router in the path is rejecting the packets with ICMP unreachables
The destination host is powered off or disconnected
The link to the destination is dropping every other packet
The destination replies, but after the 2-second timeout
questions.explanation: U is an ICMP destination unreachable returned by a router. Routers rate-limit those messages, so the probes in between time out and print periods. A powered-off host on a working path would give .....

questions.question: A standard ping from R1 to host B in a remote subnet succeeds. Host A sits on R1's LAN and is the one with the problem. Which of these has the ping NOT tested? (Choose three.)
choices: The route from host B's subnet back to host A's subnet
ACLs that filter only host A's address
Host A's default gateway setting
R1's route to host B's subnet
Host B's default gateway setting
questions.explanation: R1 sources the ping from its outgoing interface, so the replies return to that address, not to host A's subnet, and host A is not involved at all. The ping does prove R1 has a route to B and that B can reply to an address in another subnet, which needs B's gateway.

questions.question: R1's G0/1 is its LAN interface (192.168.1.1). Type a one-line ping to 10.2.2.50 that uses G0/1 as the source, to test the return route to the LAN.
questions.explanation: The source keyword makes the echo requests carry the LAN address, so the replies must be routed back to 192.168.1.0/24. Typing ping alone and answering the extended prompts does the same.

questions.question: Match each interface status (line / protocol) to its usual cause.

pairs.right: No cable, a bad cable, or the far end is off
A Layer 2 problem such as an encapsulation mismatch
A feature such as port security or BPDU guard shut the port

questions.explanation: The first status is Layer 1, the second Layer 2. Only up/up passes traffic, and err-disabled needs the cause removed plus shutdown and no shutdown.

questions.question: Which interface in the exhibit most likely has a Layer 2 problem, such as mismatched encapsulation?
questions.code:
R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.12.1       YES NVRAM  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     192.168.1.1     YES NVRAM  administratively down down
GigabitEthernet0/2     10.1.13.1       YES NVRAM  down                  down
Serial0/0/0            10.1.14.1       YES manual up                    down
choices: GigabitEthernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/2
Serial0/0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0
questions.explanation: Up/down means Layer 1 works but the data link protocol does not, typically PPP on one end and HDLC on the other. G0/1 is shut down and G0/2 has a physical problem.

questions.question: SW2 Gi0/2 is configured with speed 100 and duplex full. SW1 Gi0/1, at the other end, shows the output below and users complain of a slow, unreliable link. What is the best fix?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces g0/1 status

Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1     Uplink to SW2      connected    trunk      a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX

SW1# show interfaces g0/1 | include late
     0 babbles, 2194 late collision, 0 deferred
choices: Replace the cable between SW1 and SW2
Configure duplex half on SW2 Gi0/2 to match SW1
Shut and re-enable SW1 Gi0/1 to clear the counters
Set SW2 Gi0/2 back to speed auto and duplex auto
questions.explanation: Setting speed and duplex on SW2 disabled autonegotiation, so SW1 sensed 100 Mbps and defaulted to half duplex. Make both ends autonegotiate or configure both identically. Forcing half duplex would remove the mismatch but cripple the link.

questions.question: What is the most likely cause of the errors on this full-duplex port?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces g0/7
GigabitEthernet0/7 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
! lines omitted for brevity
  Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
! lines omitted for brevity
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     2381 input errors, 2377 CRC, 4 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
! lines omitted for brevity
     0 output errors, 0 collisions, 1 interface resets
     0 babbles, 0 late collision, 0 deferred
choices: A damaged cable or electrical interference
A duplex mismatch
Frames larger than 1518 bytes
The wrong access VLAN
questions.explanation: CRC errors climbing with zero collisions on a full-duplex link point to the physical medium. A duplex mismatch shows late collisions on the half-duplex side, and oversized frames are counted as giants.

questions.question: PC5 on Gi0/5 should be in VLAN 10 with the Sales hosts. Gi0/1 is the uplink to the distribution switch. Based on the exhibit, what is wrong?

1    default                          active    Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/6, Gi0/7, Gi0/8

1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup
1005 trnet-default                    act/unsup

VLAN 10 is not active on SW1
Gi0/5 is an access port in VLAN 99 instead of VLAN 10
PC5 needs a voice VLAN to join VLAN 10
questions.explanation: show vlan brief lists Gi0/5 under VLAN 99 (PARKING). Gi0/1 is absent because it is a trunk, which is normal, and VLAN 10 is active with three ports.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode for Gi0/5. Type the command that makes it an access port member of VLAN 10.
questions.explanation: switchport access vlan sets the VLAN the port belongs to as an access port. Pair it with switchport mode access so the port never negotiates trunking.

-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports

It is connected directly to access port Gi0/6

questions.question: Gi0/8 is cabled to a working device but does not appear anywhere in the exhibit. Which two explanations are possible? (Choose two.)

---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------

10   SALES                            active    Gi0/6, Gi0/7

1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup

Gi0/8 is assigned to a VLAN that does not exist on SW1
Gi0/8 is administratively shut down
Gi0/8 has a duplex mismatch
Gi0/8 is an access port in VLAN 1
questions.explanation: show vlan brief lists access ports in existing VLANs, whether or not they are up. Trunks are never listed, and a port whose access VLAN does not exist is inactive and also disappears. A shut down or mismatched access port would still be listed.

questions.question: Which command shows a port's configured and operational switchport mode together with its access and voice VLANs?
choices: show vlan brief
show interfaces switchport
show interfaces status
show mac address-table
questions.explanation: show interfaces <id> switchport lists Administrative Mode, Operational Mode, Access Mode VLAN, Voice VLAN and the trunk native VLAN for one port or all ports.

questions.question: Hosts in VLAN 10 on SW1 cannot reach VLAN 10 hosts on SW2 across Gi0/24, while VLAN 20 works. Based on the exhibit, why?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/24      on               802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/24      1-9,11-4094

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/24      1,20,30,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/24      1,20,30,99
choices: VLAN 10 has been removed from the allowed list on Gi0/24
Spanning tree is blocking VLAN 10 on Gi0/24
The native VLAN does not match SW2
Gi0/24 is not trunking
questions.explanation: The first list, Vlans allowed on trunk, skips 10 (1-9,11-4094), so configuration removed it. Restore it with switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10. STP blocking would remove it only from the third list.

questions.question: VLAN 10 hosts on this switch cannot use the trunk. Based on the exhibit, what is the cause?
questions.code:
SW2# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       desirable        802.1q         trunking      1

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       1-4094

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       1,20,30

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       1,20,30

VLAN 10 is pruned by VTP on Gi0/1
VLAN 10 does not exist on SW2, or it is shut down
Spanning tree blocks VLAN 10 on Gi0/1
questions.explanation: VLAN 10 is allowed (list 1 is 1-4094) but missing from list 2, which drops VLANs that are not defined or are shut down on this switch. Pruning and STP blocking would only remove it from list 3.

questions.question: SW1 Gi0/1 is also configured as dynamic auto. Based on the exhibit from SW2, what is happening on the link and how do you fix it?
questions.code:
SW2# show interfaces g0/2 switchport
Name: Gi0/2
Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: dynamic auto
Operational Mode: static access
Administrative Trunking Encapsulation: dot1q
Operational Trunking Encapsulation: native
Negotiation of Trunking: On
Access Mode VLAN: 1 (default)
Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 1 (default)

The native VLAN is mismatched; set native VLAN 99 on both ends
DTP is disabled on SW2; remove switchport nonegotiate from Gi0/2
It is an access link in VLAN 1; set switchport mode trunk on at least one end
questions.explanation: Operational Mode: static access proves the port is not trunking. Dynamic auto is passive, so two auto ends never negotiate. Configure trunk (or desirable) on at least one side; best practice is switchport mode trunk on both.

GigabitEthernet1/0/24
VLAN 99

questions.question: What is happening on Gi0/3?

SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 20 | begin Interface
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Root FWD 4         128.1    P2p
Gi0/2               Desg FWD 4         128.2    P2p
Gi0/3               Desg BKN*4         128.3    P2p *ROOT_Inc

It is an alternate port, which is normal
Loop guard blocked it because BPDUs stopped arriving
Root guard is blocking it until superior BPDUs stop arriving
questions.explanation: *ROOT_Inc marks root guard's root-inconsistent state: a switch beyond Gi0/3 is claiming to be a better root. Root guard blocks the port without err-disabling it and releases it automatically. Loop guard shows *LOOP_Inc, and BPDU guard shows err-disabled.

questions.question: A user plugged a small switch into the conference room port. After the switch is removed, what brings Gi0/12 back?
questions.code:
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port GigabitEthernet0/12 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Gi0/12, putting Gi0/12 in err-disable state

SW1# show interfaces g0/12 status

Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/12    Conf room          err-disabled 10           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
choices: Nothing; it recovers by itself when BPDUs stop
Disabling PortFast on Gi0/12
shutdown followed by no shutdown on Gi0/12
Raising the port security maximum on Gi0/12
questions.explanation: BPDU guard err-disables the port, and err-disabled ports stay down until you bounce them (or errdisable recovery is configured). Self-recovery describes root guard, not BPDU guard.

questions.question: Both switches have channel-group 1 configured on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2. What is the most likely reason for this output?

------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------
1      Po1(SD)         LACP      Gi0/1(I)    Gi0/2(I)
choices: The ports are bundled and in use
Both switches use mode passive, so neither starts LACP negotiation
The ports are suspended because their speeds differ
Po1 is a Layer 3 EtherChannel
questions.explanation: SD means Po1 is down, and I means each port is stand-alone because negotiation never succeeded. Passive on both ends is a classic cause. Mismatched settings would show s (suspended), and a working channel shows SU with P.

questions.question: Which settings must match on all member ports for them to bundle into one EtherChannel? (Choose three.)
choices: Speed and duplex
Access or trunk mode, and the allowed VLAN list
The access VLAN or the trunk native VLAN
The interface description
Whether CDP is enabled
questions.explanation: Members must look identical to the switch: speed, duplex, switchport mode, VLANs and allowed lists. A mismatched port is suspended (s). Descriptions and CDP do not affect bundling.

questions.question: You are in a simlet with four switches and need to find the root bridge for VLAN 10, starting on SW1. Put the steps in order.
items: Run show spanning-tree vlan 10 on SW1 and look for This bridge is the root
If SW1 is not the root, note its root port
Use CDP to find which switch is on the other end of that root port
Run show spanning-tree vlan 10 on that neighbor
Repeat until a switch reports This bridge is the root
questions.explanation: The root bridge has no root port, and every root port points one hop closer to it. Chasing root ports finds the root in a few commands instead of checking switches at random.

questions.question: Using the exhibit, which route does R1 use for a packet to 10.2.2.10?
questions.code:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
! lines omitted for brevity

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.1.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.1.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
L        10.1.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/2
O        10.2.2.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:14:07, GigabitEthernet0/0
S        10.2.2.0/26 [1/0] via 10.1.13.3
      192.168.1.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        192.168.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
choices: S 10.2.2.0/26 via 10.1.13.3, because it is the longest matching prefix
O 10.2.2.0/24 via 10.1.12.2, because it was learned dynamically
O 10.2.2.0/24, because the /26 route has a lower metric
None; R1 has no gateway of last resort
questions.explanation: 10.2.2.10 falls inside 10.2.2.0/26 (10.2.2.0 to 10.2.2.63) and inside the /24. The longest prefix, /26, wins regardless of AD. The default route matters only when nothing matches.

questions.question: The host can reach other hosts in its own subnet but nothing beyond it. What is the cause?
questions.code:
C:\> ipconfig

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:

   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . :
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.130
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.128
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.1.1
choices: The subnet mask should be 255.255.255.0 for this gateway
The gateway 192.168.1.1 is outside the host's subnet, 192.168.1.128/25
The host has an APIPA address and never reached DHCP
The router is missing a route to 192.168.1.128/25
questions.explanation: With a /25 mask, 192.168.1.130 lives in 192.168.1.128 to 192.168.1.255. The gateway 192.168.1.1 sits in the other half, so the host cannot reach it. The gateway must be an address in 192.168.1.129 to 192.168.1.254.

questions.question: Hosts in VLAN 20 cannot reach their gateway 192.168.20.1, while VLAN 10 works. Based on the exhibit, what is wrong?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | section interface GigabitEthernet0/0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no ip address
 duplex auto
 speed auto
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
choices: G0/0 needs an IP address for the subinterfaces to work
G0/0.20 tags frames with VLAN 30 instead of VLAN 20
Subinterface numbers must match the VLAN number exactly
The VLAN 20 gateway must be 192.168.20.254
questions.explanation: encapsulation dot1Q 30 makes G0/0.20 send and accept VLAN 30 frames, so VLAN 20 hosts never reach it. The subinterface number is only a label; the dot1Q tag is what must match the VLAN.

questions.question: Why is the static route missing from R1's routing table?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | include ip route
ip route 10.5.5.0 255.255.255.0 10.1.13.3
R1# show ip interface brief | include 0/2
GigabitEthernet0/2     10.1.13.1       YES NVRAM  down                  down
R1# show ip route 10.5.5.0
% Network not in table
choices: Static routes must name an exit interface as well as a next hop
10.5.5.0/24 must be advertised by OSPF first
G0/2 is down, so R1 has no connected route to reach the next hop 10.1.13.3
A static route needs an AD configured before it is installed
questions.explanation: IOS installs a static route only when the next hop is reachable. With G0/2 down, 10.1.13.0/30 disappears, so 10.1.13.3 is unreachable and the route is withdrawn until the interface comes back.

questions.question: What is the administrative distance of this route?
questions.explanation: The bracket holds [administrative distance/metric]: 110 is OSPF's default AD and 2 is the OSPF cost.

questions.question: R1 and R2 never list each other in show ip ospf neighbor. Based on the exhibit, why?
questions.code:
R1# show ip ospf interface g0/0 | include Area|Timer
  Internet Address 10.1.12.1/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5

R2# show ip ospf interface g0/0 | include Area|Timer
  Internet Address 10.1.12.2/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 5, Dead 20, Wait 20, Retransmit 5
choices: They are in different areas
Their addresses are in different subnets
Their hello and dead timers do not match
Their router IDs are the same
questions.explanation: Both are in area 0 and in 10.1.12.0/30, but hello and dead intervals must match exactly, so each router ignores the other's hellos. Fix it with matching ip ospf hello-interval and dead-interval values.

questions.question: R3 is on a shared Ethernet segment with three other OSPF routers. What does the exhibit show?
questions.code:
R3# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
1.1.1.1           1   FULL/DR         00:00:35    10.1.1.1        GigabitEthernet0/0
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:31    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
4.4.4.4           1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:38    10.1.1.4        GigabitEthernet0/0
choices: Normal: two DROTHERs stay in 2WAY with each other
R3 and 4.4.4.4 have mismatched hello timers
R3 and 4.4.4.4 have an interface MTU mismatch
R3 is the DR and should be FULL with every router
questions.explanation: On a broadcast segment, DROTHERs form full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR. 2WAY between two DROTHERs is expected. Mismatched timers would hide the neighbor entirely, and an MTU problem shows EXSTART or EXCHANGE.

questions.question: R1 and R2 are configured as an HSRP pair for the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN. What does the exhibit indicate?
questions.code:
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/1       10   110 P Active  local           unknown         192.168.1.254

R2# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/1       10   100   Active  local           unknown         192.168.1.254
choices: Normal operation, because R1 has the higher priority
Preemption is missing on R2, so both claim the role
The routers cannot hear each other's HSRP hellos
The two routers use different virtual IP addresses
questions.explanation: Two Active routers with Standby unknown means neither hears the other. Look at the Layer 2 path between them (VLAN, trunk, port state) and at HSRP group settings. The virtual IPs match, and preemption only decides who takes over when both are talking.

questions.question: R1 has just recovered from a reload. It has the higher priority, yet R2 (192.168.1.3) stays active. Why?
questions.code:
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/1       10   110   Standby 192.168.1.3     local           192.168.1.254
choices: R2 has a higher priority than R1
R1 and R2 use different group numbers
The virtual IP is configured on R2 only
Preemption is not configured on R1
questions.explanation: The P column is empty for R1, so it waits as Standby even with priority 110. Adding standby 10 preempt on R1 lets it reclaim the active role.

questions.question: Type the command that lists each OSPF neighbor with its router ID, state and interface.
questions.explanation: show ip ospf neighbor shows one line per neighbor: Neighbor ID, priority, state with DR/BDR role, dead time, the neighbor's address and your interface.

questions.question: G0/1 faces the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN and G0/0 faces the ISP. Users cannot reach the internet. Based on the exhibit, what is wrong?
questions.code:
R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 0 (0 static, 0 dynamic; 0 extended)
Peak translations: 0
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0
Hits: 0  Misses: 0
! lines omitted for brevity
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 refcount 0
choices: ip nat inside and ip nat outside are swapped on G0/1 and G0/0
The overload keyword is missing from the NAT rule
Access list 1 must be an extended ACL for NAT
PAT cannot translate to an interface address
questions.explanation: The LAN interface is marked outside and the ISP interface inside, so traffic from the LAN never enters NAT from an inside interface and nothing is translated. Swap the two commands.

questions.question: Match each NAT term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The inside host's address as used inside, usually private
The inside host's address as the internet sees it
The outside host's address as seen from inside, usually the same as outside global

questions.explanation: Inside or outside says whose address it is; local or global says which side of the router is looking. For source NAT, only the inside host's address changes.

questions.question: The first three inside hosts reach the internet; a fourth host cannot. Based on the exhibit, why?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config | include nat
 ip nat inside
 ip nat outside
ip nat pool PUB 203.0.113.10 203.0.113.12 netmask 255.255.255.248
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB

R1# show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global         Inside local          Outside local         Outside global
--- 203.0.113.10          192.168.1.10          ---                   ---
--- 203.0.113.11          192.168.1.11          ---                   ---
--- 203.0.113.12          192.168.1.12          ---                   ---
choices: Access list 1 permits only three inside hosts
The netmask on the pool does not match the addresses
Dynamic NAT needs a static entry for each new host
The pool has three addresses and no overload, so all are in use
questions.explanation: Without overload, dynamic NAT maps one inside host to one pool address. Three addresses serve three hosts at a time. Add overload to the ip nat inside source command (PAT) or enlarge the pool.

questions.question: Hosts on R1's G0/1 LAN receive 169.254.x.x addresses. The DHCP server is 10.9.9.9 in the data center, reached through G0/0. What is the fix?
questions.code:
R1# show ip interface g0/1
GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet address is 192.168.10.1/24
  Broadcast address is 255.255.255.255
  Address determined by non-volatile memory
  MTU is 1500 bytes
  Helper address is not set
! lines omitted for brevity
choices: Add ip helper-address 10.9.9.9 on G0/0
Add ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 on R1
Configure ip address dhcp on G0/1
Add ip helper-address 10.9.9.9 on G0/1
questions.explanation: The clients' DHCP Discover broadcasts arrive on G0/1 and stop there. ip helper-address on G0/1 relays them as unicasts to 10.9.9.9. On G0/0 it would never see the broadcasts.

questions.question: R1 is synchronized. What is the stratum of the server it synchronizes to?
questions.code:
R1# show ntp status
Clock is synchronized, stratum 3, reference is 10.9.9.123
nominal freq is 250.0000 Hz, actual freq is 250.0000 Hz, precision is 2**21
! lines omitted for brevity

R1# show ntp associations

  address         ref clock       st   when   poll reach  delay  offset   disp
*~10.9.9.123      10.9.9.1         2     33     64   377  1.204   0.315  1.902
 * sys.peer, # selected, + candidate, - outlyer, x falseticker, ~ configured
questions.explanation: The st column shows the server at stratum 2, and a client is one stratum below its server, so R1 reports stratum 3. The asterisk marks 10.9.9.123 as the server in use, and reach 377 means every recent poll was answered.

questions.question: Which command on an IOS DHCP server lists the addresses it has leased and the clients that hold them?
choices: show ip dhcp pool
show ip dhcp conflict
show ip dhcp binding
show ip interface
questions.explanation: show ip dhcp binding lists each leased address with the client ID or MAC and the lease expiry. The pool command shows counts per pool, and conflict lists addresses found already in use.

questions.question: Hosts in 10.1.5.0/24, also behind R1, cannot reach anything behind R2. Based on the exhibit, why?
questions.code:
R2# show ip interface g0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet address is 10.1.12.2/30
! lines omitted for brevity
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is 101

R2# show access-lists
Extended IP access list 101
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.50 eq www (214 matches)
    20 deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any (37 matches)
    30 permit ospf any any (1290 matches)
choices: Line 20 denies them along with 10.1.1.0/24
No line matches them, so the implicit deny drops their packets
Line 30 drops them because they are not OSPF packets
The ACL is applied in the wrong direction for them
questions.explanation: Lines 10 and 20 match only 10.1.1.0/24 sources and line 30 only OSPF, so packets from 10.1.5.0/24 reach the invisible deny any at the end. Add a permit for that subnet before the end of the ACL.

questions.question: The policy says host 10.1.1.25 must not use SSH, yet it still can. What is the fix?
questions.code:
R1# show access-lists 120
Extended IP access list 120
    10 permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any (5120 matches)
    20 deny tcp host 10.1.1.25 any eq 22
    30 deny ip any any (12 matches)
choices: Change line 30 to permit ip any any
Apply the ACL in the other direction
Add the host deny before line 10, for example as sequence 5
Replace line 20 with deny tcp any host 10.1.1.25 eq 22
questions.explanation: ACLs stop at the first match. Line 10 permits all of 10.1.1.0/24, including 10.1.1.25, so line 20 never matches (its counter has no matches). The specific deny must come before the broad permit.

questions.question: What happened on Gi0/3, and what restores it once the cause is removed?
questions.code:
SW1# show port-security interface g0/3
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
SecureStatic Address Aging : Disabled
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 0
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0050.7966.6812:10
Security Violation Count   : 1
choices: An unknown MAC appeared; it stays err-disabled until shutdown and no shutdown
The port works normally and silently drops one unknown device
The sticky MAC address expired and will be relearned automatically
The port is in restrict mode and only logs each violation
questions.explanation: Secure-shutdown with Violation Mode Shutdown and a count of 1 means the port is err-disabled after a frame from an unknown MAC. Remove the extra device (or raise the maximum), then shutdown and no shutdown.

questions.question: Which two statements about Gi0/4 are true? (Choose two.)
questions.code:
SW1# show port-security interface g0/4
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Restrict
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
SecureStatic Address Aging : Disabled
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 0
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0200.3333.3333:10
Security Violation Count   : 37
choices: The port still forwards traffic from its allowed MAC address
Frames from at least one other MAC address have been dropped
The port is err-disabled and needs shutdown and no shutdown
Protect mode would show the same violation count
The port allows two MAC addresses
questions.explanation: Restrict keeps the port Secure-up, drops frames from unknown MACs, logs them and counts them (37 here). Shutdown mode would err-disable the port, and protect mode does not increment the counter.

questions.question: Put the ACL troubleshooting steps in order.
items: Find which interfaces have ACLs and in which direction (show ip interface)
Display each ACL with its match counters (show access-lists)
Work out which line the failing traffic matches first
Send test traffic and watch which counter increases
Fix the ACL and test again
questions.explanation: Location and direction first, then contents, then first-match analysis confirmed by counters. Checking contents before location wastes time on ACLs the traffic never crosses.
